title: Implement binary search (iterative) — maintain left and right pointers, calculate mid, compare and narrow down.

s1_definition.profdef: Iterative binary search finds a target in a sorted array using a loop and two pointers, left and right, that bound the active range, without recursion. Each iteration computes the midpoint, compares it to the target, and moves either the left or right pointer to discard half the range. It runs in logarithmic time and, unlike the recursive form, uses only constant extra space because there is no call stack growth.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India searching a sorted ledger with two bookmarks, one at the first page in range and one at the last. She flips to the page exactly between the bookmarks. If the account she wants is earlier, she moves the right bookmark to just before that page; if it is later, she moves the left bookmark to just after. She keeps flipping to the new middle, tightening the bookmarks, until she lands on the account or the bookmarks cross, meaning it is not there. She never needs a stack of notes — just the two bookmarks.
s1_definition.oneliner: Iterative binary search tightens left and right pointers in a loop, halving the sorted range each step with no recursion.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Iterative binary search finds a target in a sorted array using a loop and two pointers, left and right, that bound the active range, without recursion. Each iteration computes the midpoint, compares it to the target, and moves either the left or right pointer to discard half the range. It runs in logarithmic time and, unlike the recursive form, uses only constant extra space because there is no call stack growth.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India searching a sorted ledger with two bookmarks, one at the first page in range and one at the last. She flips to the page exactly between the bookmarks. If the account she wants is earlier, she moves the right bookmark to just before that page; if it is later, she moves the left bookmark to just after. She keeps flipping to the new middle, tightening the bookmarks, until she lands on the account or the bookmarks cross, meaning it is not there. She never needs a stack of notes — just the two bookmarks.

**One line to remember:** Iterative binary search tightens left and right pointers in a loop, halving the sorted range each step with no recursion.

sections.s2_technical:
The iterative version is usually preferred over the recursive one in production because it avoids the overhead and stack-overflow risk of recursive calls, using a plain loop with constant memory.

The loop condition is `while (left <= right)`, which keeps searching as long as the range is valid. Inside, the overflow-safe midpoint is `int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;`. The comparison decides the move: on a match we return mid immediately, on the target being larger we do `left = mid + 1;` to search the right half, and on it being smaller we do `right = mid - 1;` to search the left half. The plus-one and minus-one are important: they exclude the already-checked mid so the range strictly shrinks and the loop cannot spin forever. When left exceeds right the loop ends and we return minus one for not found.

A subtle correctness point is the boundary. Using left less than or equal to right, with mid plus one and mid minus one, is the standard template that handles ranges of size one correctly and always terminates. Off-by-one mistakes here, such as using less than instead of less than or equal, cause the search to miss elements or loop forever, so the exact template matters.

A senior-level point is that the same iterative skeleton adapts to find the leftmost or rightmost match among duplicates by adjusting when you stop and which direction you keep searching, and to find a lower or upper bound. Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` is iterative internally. Because it is constant space and cache-friendly, the iterative form is the right default; I reach for recursion only when it makes a variant clearer, never for the basic lookup.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a sorted array of transaction IDs and must confirm whether a specific ID was processed, at very high throughput and with tight memory limits per request. The iterative binary search gives logarithmic lookups using only a couple of integer variables, with no recursion overhead, which suits a hot path that runs millions of times.

Problem 2 — Because the service runs in a constrained environment, we must avoid any risk of deep recursion consuming the call stack. The iterative loop uses constant extra space regardless of input size, eliminating that risk entirely.

In our mini-project we build a `TxnIndex` with an iterative `indexOf` method over a sorted array of transaction IDs. The demo searches for a present and an absent ID, logging the left and right pointers at each iteration to show the range shrinking.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the sorted array 101, 205, 309, 412, 530, 644, 701, 888, searching for 530 then 600.

Step 1: For 530, left is zero and right is seven. Mid is three, value 412. Since 412 is less than 530, we move left to four, discarding the left half including index three.

Step 2: Now left four, right seven. Mid is five, value 644. Since 644 is greater than 530, we move right to four, discarding the right half including index five.

Step 3: Now left four, right four. Mid is four, value 530. It matches, so we return index four. Three iterations for eight elements, exactly the logarithmic behaviour.

Step 4: For 600, left zero, right seven, mid three value 412, less than 600, so left becomes four.

Step 5: Left four, right seven, mid five value 644, greater than 600, so right becomes four. Left four, right four, mid four value 530, less than 600, so left becomes five.

Step 6: Now left five is greater than right four, so the loop ends. The target 600 was never found, so we return minus one. Throughout, only the two integer pointers changed, confirming constant extra space.

```
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=0 right=7 mid=3 value=412
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=4 right=7 mid=5 value=644
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=4 right=4 mid=4 value=530
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO    Txn 530 at index: 4
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=0 right=7 mid=3 value=412
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=4 right=7 mid=5 value=644
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO      left=4 right=4 mid=4 value=530
[2026-10-26 21:00:02] INFO    Txn 600 at index: -1 (-1 means not processed)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  sorted: [101, 205, 309, 412, 530, 644, 701, 888]
            0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7

  search 530 (loop, no recursion):
    left=0 right=7 mid=3(412) <530 → left=4
    left=4 right=7 mid=5(644) >530 → right=4
    left=4 right=4 mid=4(530) =530 → FOUND at 4

  pointers only (constant space): (0,7)→(4,7)→(4,4)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Iterative binary search finds a target in a sorted array using a loop and two pointers, left and right, that bound the active range, without any recursion. On each iteration I compute the midpoint, compare the middle element to the target, and move either the left pointer past the midpoint or the right pointer below it to discard half the range. Because each step halves the range, it runs in logarithmic time, and because it uses only a couple of integer variables, it uses constant extra space.

I always get the template exactly right because the boundaries are where bugs hide. The loop runs while left is less than or equal to right. The midpoint is left plus the quantity right minus left over two, which avoids the integer overflow that the naive left plus right over two can cause. When I move a pointer I use mid plus one or mid minus one to exclude the already-checked middle, which guarantees the range strictly shrinks and the loop always terminates. When left finally exceeds right, the target is absent and I return minus one.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used the iterative form on a hot path that confirms whether a specific transaction ID exists in a sorted array, running millions of times under tight memory limits. The iterative version suits this perfectly because it is constant space with no call-stack growth, so there is zero risk of a stack overflow and the constant factors are tiny and cache-friendly.

The senior-level point I make is that I prefer the iterative form as the default over recursion for plain lookups, and that the same skeleton adapts to richer variants. By adjusting when I stop and which direction I keep searching, the identical loop finds the leftmost or rightmost occurrence among duplicates, or a lower or upper bound. Java's own Arrays.binarySearch is iterative internally for exactly these reasons, so the iterative template is both the practical and the idiomatic choice.
